## Personality

Tough, practical and cheerful in any weather. She can gut a fish and an argument in one stroke.

## Lore

Agatha is thirty-seven, a river fisher of the Riverside, and she is out on the water in any weather, cheerful in all of it. She can gut a fish in one stroke and an argument in another, and people who have watched her do both say the second is quicker. Her boat is small, flat and patched, her hands are hard as rope, and her laugh carries clear across the river to the far bank.

### Her father's nets

She was born on the river. Her father Osmund has poled the ferry across it since he was a boy, and in the years when the ferry did not keep him busy enough, he fished as well, with a set of heavy nets he had mended so many times that hardly a knot of the first ones is left. Her mother, Edda, died when Agatha was fifteen, and after that it was the two of them, Osmund and his daughter, on the water every day. He taught her to read the river the way he reads it: its colour, its smell, the way it moves before rain. He did it almost entirely without words. Agatha does the talking for both of them now, and she says she has never once misunderstood a nod.

When his hands grew too stiff for the nets, Osmund gave them to her. They are her father's old nets still, and she mends them every evening on the step of the house, the way he did.

### The market and the family

She sells her catch to her husband, Silas, who keeps a fish stall in the Crown Market and names every fish he sells. They met across that stall, when Agatha came up from the river with a basket of eels and told him his prices were a disgrace, and Silas, who is loud, salty and endlessly cheerful, told her hers were worse. They have been married eleven years and they still argue about prices, loudly and with enormous enjoyment, in front of anyone who happens to be buying.

Their son Robin is a mudlark who combs the bank at low water for treasure. He is muddy, curious and certain that every shiny thing is a lost crown, and Agatha is privately very proud of him. She makes him keep to two rules: never alone at the deep end of the bank, and never after dark.

### The torn nets

Lately the nets have been coming up torn. Not snagged on a sunken branch, not chewed by a pike, not frayed with age: torn. The rents are long and ragged, sometimes through three or four rows of mesh at once, and they come up empty around the hole, as if the fish had been taken out of the net before the net was taken out of the water. Agatha has fished this river her whole life and knows every fish in it. Whatever is doing this is none of them.

She has not made a fuss. She is practical, and making a fuss does not mend nets. But she has noticed that her father, who has crossed the river after dark all his life, no longer does, and she has noticed that he will not tell her why, and she has quietly moved her own fishing to the shallower water close to the bank. Silas has started hiring guards to ride with the harbour carts because of the monsters on the roads, and over supper, half joking, he has asked her whether the river needs guards too. She told him not to be daft. She has been thinking about it ever since.

### What she wants and fears

Agatha wants her nets to come up whole and full, the way they did when she was a girl. She fears for her father, who is not as young as he behaves, and for Robin, who is braver than he should be at the water's edge.

A quest might begin with Agatha asking someone to watch the deep water with her from the boat one evening, or with a net that comes up holding something that is not a fish.
